Baby Ignus - a medical wonder

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When a baby from Heidelberg was born with a rare condition causing a severe breathing problem, a heart and lung machine was his only chance to survive, but the treatment was not without its risks.

Unique Selling Point:
For the first time in South Africa a baby born with a rare condition survived thanks to a dangerous and risky treatment he received, which in the end saved his life. It was a medical wonder as the treatment is not widely used in South Africa due to the risks involved, especially for neonates. But baby Ignus responded well and is now on the road of recovery.


Summary:
Baby Ignus Greyling was born with a rare conduction of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). This meant part of his diaphragm was missing and his bowls had moved into his chest resulting in his lungs never developing to its full capacity.

At birth he was very distressed and could not breath and was rushed to the intensive care unit for life support. The XRays showed the bowel in the left chest and a very small lung. The life support soon starting failing. There was only one option left: put baby Ignus on a heart and lung machine, called Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO). The treatment is not well known in South Africa in neonates as it carries a huge risk and complications for babies.

After two weeks, the pediatric surgeon was able to operate on the baby, pushing the intestines back and patching up the missing diaphragm. The lung was still not strong enough; another week of ECMO treatment was needed.

It was day 47 when Nadia walked into the hospital and up the stairs to the ICU ward. A miracle awaited her on the other side of the doors. Baby Ignus was off life support and for the first time she held her baby boy. Tears streamed down her cheeks as she looked at the miracle she held in her arms.


Further information:
Nadia and Philip Greyling live on a farm outside Heidelberg. She is a grade five teacher and he is a born and bred farmer. When she was pregnant with her first child, there were no complications and the birth went without a hitch. Seven years later, they thought of having a second child as their son kept asking for a brother to play with. This time Nadia changed doctors and went to a gynecologist in Alberton. Scans performed on the pregnancy showed no abnormalities and on 15 April Nadia underwent a cesarean at the Clinton Netcare hospital in Alberton where baby Ignus was born.

“The first cry is the most beautiful sound ever,’ she remembered saying to her husband looking at their perfectly formed baby. But within minutes his breathing became laboured. He was rushed to the ICU and put on a ventilator. At first Nadia had no idea what was wrong with her baby but after a series of xrays the parents were told that their baby had a rare birth defect called congenital diaphragmatic hernia or CDH. There was a large piece of diaphragm missing and during pregnancy the intestines moved into the chest preventing the left lung from developing normally. This is a life-threatening illness and most babies are unable to breathe well enough on their own because their lungs are underdeveloped and prevented from expanding in the chest area.

“Most babies placed on a breathing machine will recover but baby Ignus was not responding well”, said Dr. Ashley Jeevarathnum, the pulmonologist who assessed the baby’s condition. “ECMO was our only option as it gave his lungs time to heal and then we can consider the operation to fix his hernia”.

“ECMO treatment is not well known in the country and even less so in neonatal cases”, says Dr. Krubin Naidoo, the pediatric cardiothoracic surgeon called on by Jeevarathnum to assist with the treatment. “A child with his severe condition of CDH could not be left to fate. We had to take the risk of ECMO treatment and hoped for the best,” he said. Because babies considered for ECMO are already very sick, they are at high risk for long-term problems, including death. Once the baby is placed on EMCO, additional risks include bleeding, blood clot formation, infection, and transfusion problems. However, most babies who need ECMO would probably die if it were not used. ECMO is a treatment that uses a pump to circulate blood through an artificial lung back into the bloodstream. The system provides heart-lung bypass support outside the baby’s body.

Thirty-two days after the birth of Ignus it was time to consider the operation. He was now on ECMO for 14 days - an unusual long time for a baby. In the hands of Dr. Charles Caripinha, an expert paediatric surgeon and highly skilled in CDH surgery, baby Ignus pulled through. “Timing was of the essence since the baby had complications, but it was teamwork that played the critical role in the whole process,” he said.

Behind closed doors, Nadia observed. “I never knew if it will be the last time that I will walk up the hospital steps and see my baby,” the mother remembered. “But after 42 days and 1008 hours of fighting, I could hold my baby for the first time,” said Nadia.

But an infection set in and baby Ignus went back on high frequency ventilation. “I was crying all the way home and asked God for a miracle,” said Nadia. Then on day 49 Jeevarathnum, who was at the baby’s side every day, sent Nadia a video clip. Ignus was on nasal oxygen and breathing normally.

The story:
The story is told through the experience of the mother who lives through this trauma of never knowing if her baby will make it but never giving up hope. The expert medical team and supporting staff played a role and each expert will share the role they played and the importance of teamwork. There are cellphone video clips and photos of the baby during his medical journey and we will pick up on the visuals when filming the interviews to sketch the family life, the hospital wards and how these two worlds have merged to give baby Ignus a new life.

Producer return flight CT to Johannesburg
Two nights accommodation
Car hire x 2 days

Script:


Script: Baby Ignus - a medical wonder
Date: 8 July 2021
Duration: 8:10
V/O Nadia and Philip Greyling live on a farm outside Heidelberg in Gauteng with their son Arlo. Arlo was born seven years ago when the couple moved to the farm. There were no complications with her first pregnancy, so when Nadia became pregnant in August last year, she felt a sense of ease.

Claire Mawisa: And how was your pregnancy, was it the same walk in the park as the first one?

Nadia Greyling: Mother - Same as the first one, I had no problems. I went to see the doctor every 6 weeks.

Claire Mawisa: Then the birth comes and how was that? Talk me through the day that he was born.

Nadia Greyling: Agh, mixed emotions because you are so excited and I had a c-section. The day that they pushed me into theatre, I told his brother, I am coming home in two days with your little brother.

V/O Nadia gave birth to a baby boy on the 15th of April at the Netcare Clinton hospital in Alberton. She named him Ignus.

Link: Everything was set and ready to welcome baby Ignus welcome home from the hospital after he was born. But nothing could prepare the Greyling family for what was in store.

Nadia Greyling: He was born at 7am in the morning and the paediatrician then took him just to observe his lungs and his breathing and my husband and I still nodded at each other and thought “oh well he is crying more than his brother because my first son almost didn’t cry.’

Claire Mawisa; When did you realise something might be wrong?

Nadia Greyling: The doctors started to sound a little bit nervous, they were checking him and it was “sister, sister, here.” They just wrapped him up, showed him to me quickly, we had a photo, it was a few seconds and they took him off to the NICU.

Claire Mawisa: So you didn't even get to hold him?

Nadia Greyling: No, no.

V/O An Xray of his chest revealed why he had difficulty breathing. His left lung was small and compressed by his bowl which had moved up into the chest during pregnancy. The condition is called Congenital diaphragmatic hernia or CDH, a rare condition that affects one in every 5000 births in the United States. There are no reliable statistics for South Africa. Worldwide only 50% of children born with CDH survive and in underdeveloped countries it is as low as 1%.

V/O Due to Covid we couldn’t film in hospital but with the help of cellphone visuals we were able to track Ignus’ medical journey and the specialists who worked behind the scenes. Dr. Ashley Jeevarathnum, a specialist in respiratory diseases, led the medical team.

Up sound: This picture here….his his bowl and his stomach that herniated into the chest moving the heart to the right side and compressing that left lung completely.

V/O The Xray showed a tiny lung and a massive hernia in the chest, placing a severe strain on the heart as well.

Dr. Ashley Jeevarathnum: Paediatric Pulmonologist - I knew the numbers and I realised what it was dealing with and I realised it was going to take a real team and a lot of hard work to get this child through.

V/O Jeevarathnum had to act quickly. He called Dr. Krubin Naidoo. He is one of the few experts in South Africa specialising in ECMO or Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for newborn babies and children. This advanced life support is a last resort when all conventional methods have failed.

Dr. Krubin Naidoo: Paediatric Cardiothoracic Surgeon - If it looks like the outcome is going to be almost certainly death then we would consider this and the reason for that is because of the intensity of the therapy that is required and the complications that could happen as with any therapy.

V/OThe machine performs the function of the heart and the lung by means of a pump and an artificial lung outside of the body. The risks of ECMO are very high.

Claire Mawisa: What was your worst fear when it came to Ignus?

Dr. Krubin Naidoo: There were so many. During the cannulation itself that we did not have the right cannula sizes; that we destroy things in areas we don’t see and only find out later; that the circuit stops working and it needs to be changed; that he may bleed uncontrollably - not from places that we see but places we don't see. Those are all concerns we deal with in this therapy.

Dr. Ashley Jeevarathnum: When a patient is on ecmo they flip like a switch. For an hour or two they remain stable and then they crash. And when they crash you need to act almost immediately.

V/O There was a high probability that his kidneys would fail. Dr Sanushka Naidoo took charge during this critical stage while he was on dialysis.

Dr. Sanushka Naido: Paediatric Nephrologist - So you can imagine a small child has a very small circulating blood volume and they needed to give him a lot of fluids and blood products in order to drive that ECMO circuit and they are at risks for what we call fluid overload and in critically ill children the amount of fluid overload have been directly related to worse outcomes so it increases your risk of death basically.

Link: Nadia Greyling made the 80km trip to a hospital in Alberton every day for 60 days to be by her baby’s side where doctors were fighting to save his life.

Nadia Greyling: I think the greatest shock was when I saw all of the things connected to this body. And they said they only do this for babies they believe have a 20% chance.

UP sound: Kyk daar op daai masjien. Op daai skerm wys hulle wat is in sy keel.

Claire Mawisa: Was there a day you had a big cry?

Nadia Greyling: About three weeks ago I was standing by his side and I was praying and saying “please just give me some hope today. On the way there Dr Ashley sent me a video. He had made a clip of him breathing on his own and I could hear him saying in the background of the video: “it is amazing.”

V/O After 12 Days on ECMO Ignus was eventually stable enough to undergo surgery. Dr. Charles Carapinha performed the operation. The bowl was moved back into the abdomen and a patch was placed where the diaphragm was missing. Ignus started to show signs of recovery and with the help of his mother’s milk gained weight.

Link: Even though Nadia wasn’t physically with her newborn they were still both on the same schedule because she would express her breast milk at the same time that he was being fed at the NICU, even if it was in the middle of the night.

Up sound..Welcome guys

Nadia Greyling: So every day I would pack his milk and think I have to get to the hospital, I have to get him his feed. I felt like I was being a mom while I was there.

Up sound: “Dankie liewe Jesus vir my boetie dat hy gesond word (Thank you dear Jesus that my brother is getting better) Dankie Liewe Jesus vir die kossies. Amen.” (Thank you dear Jesus for the food. Amen)

Nadia Greyling: So on day 49 I held him for the first time. I could feel his little hand, so that was quite emotional.

Claire: You would never take his cry for granted?.

Nadia; No, no.

Claire: That in itself is a blessing.

Nadia Greyling: Yes because new mommies would come into the maternity ward and they would hear their babies crying and I just wished I could hear mine.

Up sound: Dis jou boetie. Se hello vir jou boetie.

V/O After 66 days at the Netclare Clinton hospital in Alberton, Ignus came home on father’s day as a gift from above.

Claire Mawisa: Is this a medical breakthrough in South Africa?

Dr. Krubin Naidoo: Yes, for South Africa, yes. Ignus is the first neonate with congenital diaphragmatic hernia that went onto ECMO and survived.

Nadia Greyling: We learnt a lot, we prayed a lot. We need to show him what a miracle he is and I have photos and videos of every day that I have been there.
____________________________________________________________________________
21 SECONDS Promo 1:
V/O When a baby was born with a 50% chance of survival due to a rare condition that affected his vital signs, doctors performed a miracle treatment and against all odds he survived.
Krubin Naidoo: Ignus is the first neonate with congenital diaphragmatic hernia that went onto ECMO and survived.

21 SECONDS Promo 2:
V/O When a mother from Heidelberg gave birth to a baby boy within minutes he stopped breathing and was rushed to ICU. It took 66 days and a team of specialists to pull him through.
Nadia Greyling: I was standing by his side and I was praying and saying “please just give me some hope today”.

11 SECONDS Prom:
V/O For the first time in South Africa a high-risk treatment was used successfully to save a baby’s life after he was born with a life-threatening condition that affected his breathing.
UP sound: It’s amazing.

SUNDAY PROMO: 21 SECONDS
Link: When a baby from Heidelberg was born with a rare condition, medical professionals knew that the life-saving procedure would come at a high risk.
Nadia Greyling: I was standing by his side and I was praying and saying “please just give me some hope today”.

V/O Jeevarathnum had to act quickly. He called Dr. Krubin Naidoo. He is one of the few experts in South Africa specialising in ECMO or Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for newborn babies and children. This advanced life support is a last resort when all conventional methods have failed. Dr. Krubin Naidoo: Paediatric Cardiothoracic Surgeon - If it looks like the outcome is going to be almost certainly death then we would consider this and the reason for that is because of the intensity of the therapy that is required and the complications that could happen as with any therapy. V/OThe machine performs the function of the heart and the lung by means of a pump and an artificial lung outside of the body. The risks of ECMO are very high. Claire Mawisa: What was your worst fear when it came to Ignus? Dr. Krubin Naidoo: There were so many. During the cannulation itself that we did not have the right cannula sizes; that we destroy things in areas we don’t see and only find out later; that the circuit stops working and it needs to be changed; that he may bleed uncontrollably - not from places that we see but places we don't see. Those are all concerns we deal with in this therapy. Dr. Ashley Jeevarathnum: When a patient is on ecmo they flip like a switch. For an hour or two they remain stable and then they crash. And when they crash you need to act almost immediately. V/O There was a high probability that his kidneys would fail. Dr Sanushka Naidoo took charge during this critical stage while he was on dialysis. Dr. Sanushka Naido: Paediatric Nephrologist - So you can imagine a small child has a very small circulating blood volume and they needed to give him a lot of fluids and blood products in order to drive that ECMO circuit and they are at risks for what we call fluid overload and in critically ill children the amount of fluid overload have been directly related to worse outcomes so it increases your risk of death basically. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When a baby from Heidelberg was born with a rare condition causing a severe breathing problem, a heart and lung machine was his only chance to survive, but the treatment was not without its risks.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: For the first time in South Africa a baby born with a rare condition survived thanks to a dangerous and risky treatment he received, which in the end saved his life. It was a medical wonder as the treatment is not widely used in South Africa due to the risks involved, especially for neonates. But baby Ignus responded well and is now on the road of recovery.
metadata.Summary: Baby Ignus Greyling was born with a rare conduction of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). This meant part of his diaphragm was missing and his bowls had moved into his chest resulting in his lungs never developing to its full capacity. At birth he was very distressed and could not breath and was rushed to the intensive care unit for life support. The XRays showed the bowel in the left chest and a very small lung. The life support soon starting failing. There was only one option left: put baby Ignus on a heart and lung machine, called Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO). The treatment is not well known in South Africa in neonates as it carries a huge risk and complications for babies. After two weeks, the pediatric surgeon was able to operate on the baby, pushing the intestines back and patching up the missing diaphragm. The lung was still not strong enough; another week of ECMO treatment was needed. It was day 47 when Nadia walked into the hospital and up the stairs to the ICU ward. A miracle awaited her on the other side of the doors. Baby Ignus was off life support and for the first time she held her baby boy. Tears streamed down her cheeks as she looked at the miracle she held in her arms.
metadata.Further information: Nadia and Philip Greyling live on a farm outside Heidelberg. She is a grade five teacher and he is a born and bred farmer. When she was pregnant with her first child, there were no complications and the birth went without a hitch. Seven years later, they thought of having a second child as their son kept asking for a brother to play with. This time Nadia changed doctors and went to a gynecologist in Alberton. Scans performed on the pregnancy showed no abnormalities and on 15 April Nadia underwent a cesarean at the Clinton Netcare hospital in Alberton where baby Ignus was born. “The first cry is the most beautiful sound ever,’ she remembered saying to her husband looking at their perfectly formed baby. But within minutes his breathing became laboured. He was rushed to the ICU and put on a ventilator. At first Nadia had no idea what was wrong with her baby but after a series of xrays the parents were told that their baby had a rare birth defect called congenital diaphragmatic hernia or CDH. There was a large piece of diaphragm missing and during pregnancy the intestines moved into the chest preventing the left lung from developing normally. This is a life-threatening illness and most babies are unable to breathe well enough on their own because their lungs are underdeveloped and prevented from expanding in the chest area. “Most babies placed on a breathing machine will recover but baby Ignus was not responding well”, said Dr. Ashley Jeevarathnum, the pulmonologist who assessed the baby’s condition. “ECMO was our only option as it gave his lungs time to heal and then we can consider the operation to fix his hernia”. “ECMO treatment is not well known in the country and even less so in neonatal cases”, says Dr. Krubin Naidoo, the pediatric cardiothoracic surgeon called on by Jeevarathnum to assist with the treatment. “A child with his severe condition of CDH could not be left to fate. We had to take the risk of ECMO treatment and hoped for the best,” he said. Because babies considered for ECMO are already very sick, they are at high risk for long-term problems, including death. Once the baby is placed on EMCO, additional risks include bleeding, blood clot formation, infection, and transfusion problems. However, most babies who need ECMO would probably die if it were not used. ECMO is a treatment that uses a pump to circulate blood through an artificial lung back into the bloodstream. The system provides heart-lung bypass support outside the baby’s body. Thirty-two days after the birth of Ignus it was time to consider the operation. He was now on ECMO for 14 days - an unusual long time for a baby. In the hands of Dr. Charles Caripinha, an expert paediatric surgeon and highly skilled in CDH surgery, baby Ignus pulled through. “Timing was of the essence since the baby had complications, but it was teamwork that played the critical role in the whole process,” he said. Behind closed doors, Nadia observed. “I never knew if it will be the last time that I will walk up the hospital steps and see my baby,” the mother remembered. “But after 42 days and 1008 hours of fighting, I could hold my baby for the first time,” said Nadia. But an infection set in and baby Ignus went back on high frequency ventilation. “I was crying all the way home and asked God for a miracle,” said Nadia. Then on day 49 Jeevarathnum, who was at the baby’s side every day, sent Nadia a video clip. Ignus was on nasal oxygen and breathing normally. The story: The story is told through the experience of the mother who lives through this trauma of never knowing if her baby will make it but never giving up hope. The expert medical team and supporting staff played a role and each expert will share the role they played and the importance of teamwork. There are cellphone video clips and photos of the baby during his medical journey and we will pick up on the visuals when filming the interviews to sketch the family life, the hospital wards and how these two worlds have merged to give baby Ignus a new life.
